papers.name: Paper 1: Speaking in French
papers.covers: Three tasks, in this order: a read aloud with a short interaction to follow (12 marks: 8 for reading the text aloud, 4 for answering two unprepared questions about it), a role play (10 marks), and a picture task (28 marks: 12 for describing one of two pictures and answering two questions, 16 for the conversation that follows). Fifteen minutes' preparation comes first, the last minute of it in the exam room to practise the read aloud out loud. Higher: 10 to 12 minutes plus the preparation, 25 to 27 minutes in all (the time shown). Foundation: 7 to 9 minutes plus the preparation, 22 to 24 minutes in all. 25% of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 2: Listening and understanding in French
papers.covers: Higher: 60 minutes; Foundation: 45 minutes; both include 5 minutes' reading time. Section A (40 marks): multiple-choice, multiple-response and short-answer questions, set in English and answered in English. Section B (10 marks): a dictation, a short passage of spoken French written down in French. Each recording is played three times, with pauses between sentences. 25% of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 3: Reading and understanding in French
papers.covers: Higher: 1 hour; Foundation: 45 minutes. Section A (40 marks): questions set in English and answered in English, eight at Higher and nine at Foundation. Section B (10 marks): translation into English, one passage at Higher and five sentences at Foundation. 25% of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 4: Writing in French
papers.covers: Instructions in English, answers in French. Higher (1 hour 20 minutes): Q1 an informal task, one of two, about 80 to 90 words (18 marks); Q2 a formal task, one of two, about 130 to 150 words, weighing pros and cons across past, present and future (22 marks); Q3 a short paragraph to translate into French (10 marks). Foundation (1 hour 15 minutes): Q1 four short sentences about a photo (8 marks); Q2 a formal task, one of two, about 40 to 50 words (14 marks); Q3 an informal task, one of two, about 80 to 90 words, the same as Higher Q1 (18 marks); Q4 five sentences to translate into French (10 marks). Word counts are recommendations: you are not penalised for writing more or fewer. 25% of the GCSE.

commandWords.meaning: Listening Section A and the Reading paper: the questions are in English, and so are your answers. The specification requires responses in English, so give the meaning in English rather than copying French words from the text.

Reading Section B: turn the French into natural English, five sentences at Foundation and a passage at Higher. Account for every word and every tense first, then read the English back to make it natural.

Listening Section B: write down in French what you hear. You are rewarded for accurate spelling, so accents and silent endings count, which is why the sounds of French have to be learnt as well as the words.

Speaking task 1: read a short French text aloud (8 marks, for pronunciation), then answer two unprepared questions about it in the present tense, giving opinions (4 marks). The last minute of your preparation, in the exam room, lets you practise it out loud first.

Speaking task 2: a transactional situation such as a hotel, a café or a station, with five prompts in English, each needing one utterance. Ask one question at Foundation and two at Higher; at Higher you also answer one question in a future timeframe. It is marked on communication only, so the formal register is not required.

Speaking task 3: choose one of two pictures and describe the people, the location and the activity; answer two unprepared questions about your own experiences and opinions (at Higher the second is in a past tense); then a conversation, worth 16 marks, starting from the same thematic context.

Writing: the instructions are in English and your answers are in French. Answer every bullet point and aim for the recommended word count: about 40 to 50 words (Foundation Q2), 80 to 90 (Foundation Q3, Higher Q1) or 130 to 150 (Higher Q2).

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Understand and respond to spoken language, in speaking and in writing. Speaking 15%, Listening 20%.
Understand and respond to written language, in speaking and in writing. Speaking 2%, Reading 25%, Writing 18%.
Demonstrate knowledge and accurate application of the grammar and vocabulary prescribed in the specification. Speaking 8%, Listening 5%, Writing 7%.

grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Answers exactly what is asked, in English, with the detail the recording gives: a time, a reason, a negative. Listens for the words that change a meaning — ne … pas, jamais, plus — rather than for familiar nouns.

Writes what French sounds become on paper: silent final consonants, accents, the -ent that is never pronounced, agreement that cannot be heard. Uses the three hearings — the whole sentence first, then the gaps, then a check.
Accounts for every word and keeps every tense, then reads the English back to make it natural. Imperfect becomes used to or was doing; depuis with the present becomes have been doing.

Pronounces French as French: silent endings left silent, liaisons made, nasal vowels kept, and the text's own punctuation used for phrasing. Uses the minute in the exam room to say the hard words aloud once.

Covers every prompt with one clear utterance each, asks the required questions (one at Foundation, two at Higher), and at Higher answers the question in a future timeframe, where je vais + infinitive is enough.

Describes the people, the location and the activity, answers the two questions with opinions and reasons (at Higher the second in a past tense), and moves between past, present and future in the conversation.

Covers every bullet point, uses a combination of present, past and future timeframes, signalled by avant, maintenant and à l'avenir, varies opinion phrases and connectives, and gets agreements and verb endings right. Range with accuracy, not length.

Covers every bullet point, weighs pros and cons and reaches a reasoned view, and moves accurately between past, present and future timeframes, using more complex structures where they add something rather than for show.
